title: Outrage grows as CDC reportedly poised to fund "unethical" vaccine trial
gist: The CDC is reportedly preparing to fund a $1.6 million trial in Guinea-Bissau that would withhold the hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine from half of 14,000 newborns, despite its suspension in January and international condemnation. The WHO and outside experts call the design unethical, and the Danish lead researchers are under misconduct investigation.

insights.claim: CDC director's office staff reportedly told the budget office in late September to set aside $1.6 million for a suspended Guinea-Bissau hepatitis B vaccine trial, per Rolling Stone.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Signals US public-health funding is being steered by political leadership toward contested research; watch for formal grant action.
insights.locator: Outrage has erupted among health experts

insights.claim: The reported $1.6 million would be pulled from CDC global health security programs that might otherwise fund responses such as the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Reallocation away from outbreak response raises global health-security and spillover risk.
insights.quote: The money was to be pulled from funding for the CDC’s global health security programs
insights.locator: The trial was suspended in January

insights.claim: The CDC, under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., appears eager to move the trial forward once Guinea-Bissau approves it.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Indicates US health policy direction under current HHS leadership; relevant to vaccine-policy and public-health political risk.
insights.locator: For now, the trial is still on hold

insights.claim: HHS, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to Ars Technica's request for comment.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: No official explanation yet, so the funding remains unconfirmed beyond press reports.
insights.locator: The Department of Health and Human Services

insights.claim: The trial would be run by University of Southern Denmark researchers Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, who received an unsolicited $1.6 million CDC grant in December and are under Danish investigation over alleged falsification and scientific misconduct.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Funding a team under misconduct investigation adds reputational and legal risk to the sponsor.
insights.locator: If the trial moves forward, it would be funded by the US

insights.claim: Studies by Stabell Benn and Aaby have been promoted by anti-vaccine advocates, drawing concern and criticism from other researchers.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Helps explain why the group's work is politically valued by vaccine skeptics.
insights.locator: If the trial moves forward, it would be funded by the US

insights.claim: The University of Southern Denmark approved the revised design, and its health sciences dean says Guinea-Bissau's ethics committee has signed off, leaving national government authorization as the final step.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The only remaining gate is Guinea-Bissau's government authorization; that decision is the event to monitor.
insights.quote: “[T]he study cannot begin until the necessary national authorization has been obtained,”
insights.locator: For now, the trial is still on hold

insights.claim: The trial would enroll 14,000 Guinea-Bissau newborns, half receiving a hepatitis B birth dose and half not, to look for alleged harms of a dose that decades of use have shown safe and effective.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Core design flaw cited by critics: randomizing away a proven standard of care.

insights.claim: Unvaccinated newborns face a high risk of chronic hepatitis B, which can lead to liver cirrhosis, liver cancer and premature death.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Quantifies the human cost behind the ethical objection.
insights.locator: Outrage has erupted among health experts

insights.claim: Outside experts argue the Declaration of Helsinki requires trials to give the best proven intervention regardless of local standard, so the argument that Guinea-Bissau does not routinely give birth doses does not justify a no-vaccine arm.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Shows the ethical standard the trial would be judged against internationally.
insights.locator: Stabell Benn and Aaby have argued

insights.claim: The WHO rebuked the trial in February, saying its premise rests on hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence and that resource constraints cannot justify withholding proven care.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Institutional condemnation raises the cost of proceeding for any funder.
insights.quote: “Resource constraints cannot be used to justify withholding proven care in a research study involving people.
insights.locator: In a scathing rebuke in February

insights.claim: Guinea-Bissau, which had a coup in November 2025, lacks resources and infrastructure for routine birth-dose vaccination and plans universal administration only from 2028.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Context for why the trial's sponsors call the unvaccinated arm a status quo, and for the country's fragility.

insights.claim: The trial design was revised to ask mothers about hepatitis B infection and test a small fraction, but this has not eased concerns that an unvaccinated group is fundamentally unethical.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Cosmetic changes do not resolve the core objection, so controversy is likely to persist.
insights.locator: According to the Rolling Stone report

insights.claim: Guinea-Bissau's health minister suspended the study in January, citing insufficient coordination for a final decision while ethical and technical reviews continued.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Shows local officials initially acted as the check on the trial.
insights.quote: “There has been no sufficient coordination in order to take a final decision regarding the study,”

insights.claim: Stand Up for Science vows to block the trial again, calling it a gross violation of human rights and bad science used against the world's most vulnerable people.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Organized opposition makes further delays or reputational fights likely.
insights.quote: “We stopped this unethical study the first time and we’ll do it again,”
insights.locator: Nonprofit advocacy group Stand Up for Science
